hops.afterHeading: Characters you can see: symmetry, layers, cavities
hops.title: The sponge that put itself back together
hops.text: In 1907 the zoologist Henry Van Peters Wilson broke a piece of living red sponge, Microciona, into fragments and pressed them through a fine mesh sieve into seawater. What came through looked like a lifeless reddish cloud. It was not. The loose cells crawled together into clumps, the clumps merged into bigger clumps, and the clumps reorganized until Wilson had small but fully working sponges. A sponge has no organs and only simple cell layers, and those cells can sort themselves back into a whole animal.

sources.citation: Ashworth, W. B., Jr. (2022). Scientist of the Day: Henry Van Peters Wilson. Linda Hall Library (on Wilson, Journal of Experimental Zoology, 1907).

image.caption: Sponge cells pushed through a sieve crawled back together and rebuilt small, working sponges.

hops.title: A jellyfish relative living in salmon muscle
hops.text: Henneguya salminicola is a microscopic parasite that forms cysts a few millimeters across in the muscle of Pacific salmon. It has no gut and none of the complex tissues you expect in an animal. In 2020 researchers found it has no mitochondrial genome at all, and its key genes for aerobic respiration, the usual way animal cells use oxygen to make ATP, are missing or broken. Yet gene comparisons place it inside Cnidaria, with jellyfish and sea anemones. One anatomical clue survives: its polar capsule closely resembles a cnidarian stinging capsule. Nearly the whole cnidarian body plan is gone, and it is still a cnidarian.

sources.citation: Yahalomi, D. et al. (2020). A cnidarian parasite of salmon (Myxozoa: Henneguya) lacks a mitochondrial genome. PNAS 117(10):5358-5363.
Chang, E. S. et al. (2015). Genomic insights into the evolutionary origin of Myxozoa within Cnidaria. PNAS 112(48):14912-14917.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A Pacific salmon in clear coastal water, with a magnifying lens showing small pale cysts in its muscle and a jellyfish drifting far behind.
image.caption: A salmon parasite with no gut and no mitochondrial genome still belongs with the jellyfish, in Cnidaria.

hops.afterHeading: What a coelom, a through gut and segments allow
hops.title: Your tongue has no bones either
hops.text: Stick out your tongue and squeeze it into a narrow point. It gets longer as it gets thinner. Your tongue has no bones and no fluid-filled coelom like an earthworm's. Instead, vertical, crosswise and lengthwise muscle fibers crisscross through it and make a tissue that is essentially incompressible, the same boneless trick octopus arms and elephant trunks use. When its muscles squeeze it both narrower and flatter, its cross-section shrinks, and because its volume stays nearly the same, it has to get longer. You just felt a constant-volume skeleton working inside your own mouth.

sources.citation: Kier, W. M. (2012). The diversity of hydrostatic skeletons. Journal of Experimental Biology 215(8):1247-1257.
Sekhavati, Sellers and Ross (2026). Biomechanics and evolution of the primate tongue. PMC13045644.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student at a desk looks into a hand mirror while sticking out a narrow pointed tongue, next to a plush octopus and a toy elephant.
image.caption: Squeezing a nearly constant-volume tongue narrower and flatter makes it longer.

audio.title: A barnacle in disguise, a slug with borrowed stingers, and a worm robot that met a hammer
audio.transcript:
Here are three stories about body plans. In each one, the body tells you a lot about how the animal lives, and much less about who its relatives are.

First, barnacles. Walk along a rocky shore and you will see them, little white cones glued to the rock. For a long time, most naturalists followed Carl Linnaeus and Georges Cuvier and filed barnacles with the molluscs, next to clams and snails. It is easy to see why. An adult barnacle cements itself in place, lives inside a hard shell, and holds seawater in a cavity around its body. It looks like a small, grumpy clam. Then, in eighteen thirty, an army surgeon and naturalist named John Vaughan Thompson published something he had seen four years earlier. In the spring of eighteen twenty-six he kept swimming barnacle larvae in a glass vessel of seawater, and one May night he found that some had stuck themselves to the bottom and turned into young barnacles. The larvae did not look like baby clams at all. They looked like the larvae of crustaceans, the group that includes crabs and lobsters. Plenty of people doubted him at first. A few years later another naturalist, Hermann Burmeister, backed him up, and barnacles slowly moved out of the molluscs. Later still, Charles Darwin spent from eighteen forty-six to eighteen fifty-four dissecting barnacles. Today they sit with the other crustaceans among the arthropods, in the moulting group, Ecdysozoa. The shell was real. It just pointed to the wrong family.

Second, a sea slug with borrowed weapons. Glaucus atlanticus is a small, bright blue slug that floats upside down at the surface of the ocean, held up by air in its stomach. It is a mollusc, a relative of snails. One of the things it hunts is the Portuguese man o' war, a venomous cnidarian. The slug eats it and stores the man o' war's stinging capsules in the tips of the finger-like projections along its sides, called cerata, where they help defend the slug. So if you sorted animals by stinging capsules alone, you would put a snail relative in with the jellyfish. And it gets stranger. In a study published in twenty twenty-five, researchers in Japan reported that slugs they raised in aquariums used their front-most cerata like hands to grab small fish. They called their paper "Blue angels have devil hands."

Third, a robot that copied the earthworm. In twenty twelve, engineers at M I T, Harvard University and Seoul National University reported on a soft robot called Meshworm. They rolled a flexible polymer mesh into a tube and wrapped it with tightly coiled nickel-titanium wire, which works like the worm's circular muscles. More wire ran along its length, like longitudinal muscles. A small electric current heats a ring of wire, the wire contracts, and that section of the tube squeezes in. Do that section after section, and a slow wave runs down the body and the robot inches forward the way a worm does. Then, to see how tough it was, the team stepped on it and hit it with a hammer several times. Built almost entirely of soft, flexible parts, Meshworm crawled away intact.

A shell that fooled the experts, stingers that came from someone else's body, and a worm design good enough for engineers to borrow. In every case, the body explains how the animal works, and the family tree needs other evidence.
